newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Insurers juggle risks and rewards of year 2000.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Insurers juggle risks and rewards of year 2000.

text.p: Insurers are eyeing the turn of the century with a mixture of fear and hope.

Like other businesses they are combing their computers to inoculate them against the "millennium bug" -- ensuring they will recognise the year 2000 and roll dates on life, motor and commercial policies a year forward rather than travel back to 1900 or worse.
They will also have to guard against picking up the tab from policyholding businesses which fail to prepare their computer systems properly for the millennium and come grinding to a halt.
However, for insurance companies, 2000 also presents an opportunity to create a market for insuring specifically against this new risk.
MOST INSURERS WELL PREPARED FOR MILLENNIUM
Since their business is risk management, it is not surprising that most insurers say they are well prepared for the moment when clocks tick over into the first seconds of 2000.
The amount of preparation needed varies between companies, with newer entrants to the market and those who computerised more recently having less to worry about than those with older systems.

Direct Line, the telephone insurer owned by Royal Bank of Scotland, foresees no problems with its own computer systems, largely because they have been built up since 1985 with the changeover to 2000 in mind.
"We recognised the potential problem many years ago and changed our systems as we went along," said Direct Line spokesman Adrian Webb.
Direct Line says the fact that it has a customer-based rather than a policy-based system, so that each customer has only one set of records, also minimises the changes needed.
But David Molyneaux, vice president, risk management, at London-based broker Minet, said that even the newest computers were linked to older systems and this trend was spreading.
Minet, a part of St Pauls Cos, is offering millennium insurance underwritten by AIG. So far, Minet has targeted this primarily at large British companies.
Awareness of the millennium problem is greater in Britain than elsewhere in Europe, but other countries are catching up, particularly Germany, Molyneaux said.
The millennium policy will offer $100-200 million cover against business interruption and protect against disruption resulting from millennium problems at other companies.
The premium is high, at around 60 percent of the cover, but much of this will be refundable if the loss experience is good, Molyneaux said.
Before taking out the policy, companies will have to submit to an audit by one of the leading consultancy groups to review their millennium preparations.
British American Financial Services, a part of the B.A.T. group, is carrying out its own internal review and has identified older systems and PCs as being the areas where most work needs to be done.
However, John Marsh, international IT and project director at BAFS, said the group was taking the opportunity to weed out some of its older PCs and standardise around fewer systems.
B.A.T. units Eagle Star and Allied Dunbar were well on the way to meeting their deadline of achieving Year 2000 compliancy by November 1998, he added.
"Meeting this target is essential for all insurers selling one year renewable policies such as private motor," Marsh said.

Marsh put the cost of millennium compliance at around 10-20 million pounds ($16-32 million) for Eagle Star, noting that much work was done when most of the company's systems were updated in the early 1990s.

General Accident too said it had everything in hand for the millennium, but noted that problems could not be ruled out altogether because of the complex nature of the task and the spread of computer links.
"I wouldn't say we're relaxed, but we've got everything in hand and we know where we're going...We should be in advance of anything going wrong," said spokesman Tony Kerfoot.

The cost of preparing for the millennium was significant, he said, but declined to put a figure on it, adding that it was planned investment spending and did not involve taking resources from other projects.
CHECKING THE WORDING
Like other insurers, General Accident will be looking at policy wording, largely to decide what to exclude from millennium-related events.
"Everybody knows it's coming and any business worth its salt is making preparations," Kerfoot said.

Others agreed that policies should not cover millennium-related incidents that should have been foreseen. Direct Line, for example would be unlikely to pay out for a 20-year-old PC which failed to work on January 1, 2000.
The millennium bug is also being addressed at industry level, with leading British insurers meeting regularly to discuss the issue.
A similar forum exists in Lloyds of London, where representatives from most of the insurance market's managing agencies are taking a strict line with software suppliers.
Kevin Wallis-Eade, IT director of Lloyd's managing agency Archer, said his company was asking system vendors and suppliers to have millennium plans in place by the end of June.

However, the millennium is only part of story. Industry experts warn that other key dates, such as September 9, 1999 -- which computer code will write as 9999 -- could also give computer systems a headache.

Meanwhile, insurers are already mulling the business opportunities presented by other compliance scenarios, such as European Monetary Union and the proposed creation of a single European currency. ($1= 0.609 British Pounds)
